![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199341/assets/c316b62d5c1a08c6513413fd87c36c6feb26fb632709909a9c9f761d0806c4af.png)

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?
feedback.worked_solution:
A type II region can be written as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,a\le y\le b,\,g(y)\le x\le f(y)\},
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of $y:$

$$
y=-2(x-3)\,⟹\,x=-\frac{y}{2}+3
$$

The function $x=-\sqrt{y}+2$ is already written as a function of $y.$

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines $y=1$ and $y=3.$ So, we have $1\le y\le 3.$

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function $g(y)$ and the right function $f(y).$ A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199341/assets/fb05eec73599c1beb8dd588c478208315f6edaf10af999115eb29fa10d5601e9.png)

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function $x=-\sqrt{y}+2$ and leaves through the upper function $x=-\frac{y}{2}+3.$ So, we have $-\sqrt{y}+2\le x\le -\frac{y}{2}+3.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,-\sqrt{y}+2\le x\le -\frac{y}{2}+3\}.
$$

feedback.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following represents the shaded region above as a type II region in two-dimensional space?

a
D={(x,y):1≤y≤3,−y+3≤x≤y2+2}
b
D={(x,y):−y+2≤y≤−y2+3,1≤x≤3}
c
D={(x,y):0≤y≤3,−y+2≤x≤2.5}
d
D={(x,y):y≤y≤y2,1≤x≤3}
e
D={(x,y):1≤y≤3,−y+2≤x≤−y2+3}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type II region can be written as

D={(x,y):a≤y≤b,g(y)≤x≤f(y)},

where f and g are continuous functions.

To express the given region as a type II region, we first rewrite all of the given curves as functions of y:

y=−2(x−3)⟹x=−y2+3

The function x=−y+2 is already written as a function of y.

Notice that the region lies between the horizontal lines y=1 and y=3. So, we have 1≤y≤3.

We draw a horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left function g(y) and the right function f(y). A horizontal line should intersect the region in a single interval only for it to be a type II region.

The horizontal line enters the region through the lower function x=−y+2 and leaves through the upper function x=−y2+3. So, we have −y+2≤x≤−y2+3.

Therefore, we obtain D={(x,y):1≤y≤3,−y+2≤x≤−y2+3}.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the finite region bounded between the ellipses $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$

I. It is a type I region

II. It is a type II region

III. It's neither a type I nor a type II region
question.worked_solution:
First, let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199341/assets/627e7e102a0f16cb0c4946e42b48ad122299d729c5bc419293e258a3f2e1701e.png)

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Solve $f(x)=0$ where $f(x)=\frac{x+5}{2{x}^{2}-5x-25}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+5}{2{x}^{2}-5x-25} \\  & =\frac{x+5}{(x-5)(2x+5)}\end{aligned}
$$

 

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =0 \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=-5.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the roots of $f(w)=\frac{{w}^{2}-w-2}{w-5}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(w)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(w)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{w}^{2}-w-2}{w-5}=0.
$$

First, we factor $f(w),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(w) & =\frac{{w}^{2}-w-2}{w-5} \\  & =\frac{(w-2)(w+1)}{w-5}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $w:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(w-2)(w+1) & =0 \\ w & =-1,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(w)=0$ are $w=-1$ and $w=2.$

questions.problem:
In **ascending order**, the roots of $g(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-16}{{x}^{2}-7x+10}$ are

questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $g(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $g(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-16}{{x}^{2}-7x+10}=0.
$$

First, we factor $g(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-16}{{x}^{2}-7x+10} \\  & =\frac{(x+4)(x-4)}{(x-2)(x-5)}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)(x-4) & =0 \\ x & =-4,\,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $g(x)=0$, in ascending order, are $x=-4$ and $x=4.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+14}{{x}^{2}-4}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+14}{{x}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{(x-7)(x-2)}{(x+2)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x-7)\cancel{(x-2)}}{(x+2)\cancel{(x-2)}} \\  & =\frac{x-7}{x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-7 & =0\,⟹\,x=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=7.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Find the roots of $f(z)=\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(z)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(z)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)(z+4)}{z(z+4)} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)\cancel{(z+4)}}{z\cancel{(z+4)}} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =0\,⟹\,z=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(z)=0$ is $z=-1.$

questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+3x-10}{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-9x+18}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3x-10}{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-9x+18} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)(x-2)}{{x}^{2}(x-2)-9(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)(x-2)}{({x}^{2}-9)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)(x-2)}{(x+3)(x-3)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)\cancel{(x-2)}}{(x+3)(x-3)\cancel{(x-2)}} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)}{(x+3)(x-3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5=0\,⟹\,x=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=-5.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
In **ascending order**, the roots of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3}$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}} $\,$
and
$\,\,x=$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x-2)-1(x-2)}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)(x-2)}{3\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(x-2)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-1,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(x)=0$, in ascending order, are $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(h)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(h)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(h) & =\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{{h}^{2}(h+3)-25(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{({h}^{2}-25)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{(h+5)(h-5)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(h+5)}(h+4)}{\cancel{(h+5)}(h-5)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{h+4}{(h-5)(h+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $h:$

$$
\begin{aligned}h+4=0\,⟹\,h=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(h)=0$ is $h=-4.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With a Linear Numerator and No Common Factors
canonical_examples.problem: Solve $f(x)=0,$ where $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x^2 + x - 6}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x+1}{{x}^{2}+x-6} \\  & =\frac{2x+1}{(x+3)(x-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

 

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & =0 \\ 2x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With a Quadratic Numerator and No Common Factors
canonical_examples.problem: Solve $f(x)=0,$ where $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2-4x}{x^2+5x+6}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-4x}{{x}^{2}+5x+6} \\  & =\frac{x(x-4)}{(x+2)(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(x-4) & =0 \\ x & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(x)=0$ are $x=0$ and $x=4.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Roots of a Rational Function With Common Factors
canonical_examples.problem: Solve $f(x)=0,$ where $f(x) = \dfrac{x+1}{x^2-x-2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}-x-2} \\  & =\frac{x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x+1)}}{\cancel{(x+1)}(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the numerator equal to zero, we get $1=0,$ which is a false statement. Therefore, $f(x)=0$ has no solution.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Roots of a Rational Function Containing a Cubic Expression
canonical_examples.problem: Solve $f(x)=0$, where $f(x) = \dfrac{x^3-2x^2-9x+18}{x^2-x-2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-9x+18}{{x}^{2}-x-2} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x-2)-9(x-2)}{(x-2)(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)({x}^{2}-9)}{(x-2)(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)(x-3)(x+3)}{(x-2)(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-2)}(x-3)(x+3)}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the numerator equal to zero and solving for $x$ gives

$$
(x-3)(x+3) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \pm3.
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(x)=0$ are $x=3$ and $x=-3.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To find the zeros of a rational function, we first need to factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve.

For example, consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{x-3}{x^2-25}.$ Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{x-3}{(x+5)(x-5)}.
$$

There are no common factors to cancel, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =0 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=3.$

EXPLANATION

First, we factor f(x), as follows:

f(x)=x+52x2−5x−25=x+5(x−5)(2x+5)

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for x:

x+5=0x=−5

Therefore, the solution to f(x)=0 is x=−5.

\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-4x}{{x}^{2}+5x+6} \\  & =\frac{x(x-4)}{(x+2)(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+14}{{x}^{2}-4}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+14}{{x}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{(x-7)(x-2)}{(x+2)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x-7)\cancel{(x-2)}}{(x+2)\cancel{(x-2)}} \\  & =\frac{x-7}{x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x-7 & =0\,⟹\,x=7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=7.$

Find the roots of f(x)=x2+3x−10x3−2x2−9x+18.

a
x=3
b
x=−5,3
c
x=−5,2
d
x=2

Submit

EXPLANATION

The roots of f(x) are the solutions to the equation f(x)=0. In our case, we have

x2+3x−10x3−2x2−9x+18=0.

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows: f(x)=x2+3x−10x3−2x2−9x+18=(x+5)(x−2)x2(x−2)−9(x−2)=(x+5)(x−2)(x2−9)(x−2)=(x+5)(x−2)(x+3)(x−3)(x−2)=(x+5)(x−2)(x+3)(x−3)(x−2)=(x+5)(x+3)(x−3)

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for x:

x+5=0⟹x=−5

Therefore, the solution to f(x)=0 is x=−5.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x-2)-1(x-2)}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)(x-2)}{3\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(x-2)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-1,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(x)=0$, in ascending order, are $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(h)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(h)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(h) & =\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{{h}^{2}(h+3)-25(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{({h}^{2}-25)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{(h+5)(h-5)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(h+5)}(h+4)}{\cancel{(h+5)}(h-5)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{h+4}{(h-5)(h+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $h:$

$$
\begin{aligned}h+4=0\,⟹\,h=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(h)=0$ is $h=-4.$

question.problem: Solve $f(x)=0$ where $f(x)=\frac{x+5}{2{x}^{2}-5x-25}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we factor $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+5}{2{x}^{2}-5x-25} \\  & =\frac{x+5}{(x-5)(2x+5)}\end{aligned}
$$

 

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =0 \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=-5.$

EXPLANATION

First, we factor f(x), as follows:

f(x)=x+52x2−5x−25=x+5(x−5)(2x+5)

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for x:

x+5=0x=−5

question.problem: Solve $f(t)=0$ where $f(t)=\frac{t-3}{{t}^{2}+6t+5}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we factor $f(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{t-3}{{t}^{2}+6t+5} \\  & =\frac{t-3}{(t+5)(t+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

 

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}t-3 & =0 \\ t & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(t)=0$ is $t=3.$

First, we factor f(t), as follows:

f(t)=t−3t2+6t+5=t−3(t+5)(t+1)

t−3=0t=3

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find the roots of $f(w)=\frac{{w}^{2}-w-2}{w-5}.$
question.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(w)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(w)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{w}^{2}-w-2}{w-5}=0.
$$

First, we factor $f(w),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(w) & =\frac{{w}^{2}-w-2}{w-5} \\  & =\frac{(w-2)(w+1)}{w-5}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $w:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(w-2)(w+1) & =0 \\ w & =-1,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(w)=0$ are $w=-1$ and $w=2.$

question.problem: Find the roots of $f(z)=\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z}.$
question.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(z)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(z)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)(z+4)}{z(z+4)} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)\cancel{(z+4)}}{z\cancel{(z+4)}} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =0\,⟹\,z=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(z)=0$ is $z=-1.$

feedback.problem: Find the roots of $f(z)=\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(z)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(z)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =\frac{{z}^{2}+5z+4}{{z}^{2}+4z} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)(z+4)}{z(z+4)} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)\cancel{(z+4)}}{z\cancel{(z+4)}} \\  & =\frac{(z+1)}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =0\,⟹\,z=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(z)=0$ is $z=-1.$

question.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$

$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Roots of a Rational Function Containing a Cubic Expression
last_observation.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+3x-10}{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-9x+18}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3x-10}{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-9x+18} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)(x-2)}{{x}^{2}(x-2)-9(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)(x-2)}{({x}^{2}-9)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)(x-2)}{(x+3)(x-3)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)\cancel{(x-2)}}{(x+3)(x-3)\cancel{(x-2)}} \\  & =\frac{(x+5)}{(x+3)(x-3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5=0\,⟹\,x=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(x)=0$ is $x=-5.$

question.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x-2)-1(x-2)}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)(x-2)}{3\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(x-2)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-1,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(x)=0$, in ascending order, are $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

In **ascending order**, the roots of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3}$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}} $\,$
and
$\,\,x=$
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(x)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(x)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}-x+2}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(x-2)-1(x-2)}{3x-3} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}{3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)(x-2)}{3\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{(x+1)(x-2)}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =-1,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(x)=0$, in ascending order, are $x=-1$ and $x=2.$

question.name: Question 10
question.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(h)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(h)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(h) & =\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{{h}^{2}(h+3)-25(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{({h}^{2}-25)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{(h+5)(h+4)}{(h+5)(h-5)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(h+5)}(h+4)}{\cancel{(h+5)}(h-5)(h+3)} \\  & =\frac{h+4}{(h-5)(h+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $h:$

$$
\begin{aligned}h+4=0\,⟹\,h=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(h)=0$ is $h=-4.$

The roots of f(h) are the solutions to the equation f(h)=0. In our case, we have

h2+9h+20h3+3h2−25h−75=0.

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

f(h)=h2+9h+20h3+3h2−25h−75=(h+5)(h+4)h2(h+3)−25(h+3)=(h+5)(h+4)(h2−25)(h+3)=(h+5)(h+4)(h+5)(h−5)(h+3)=(h+5)(h+4)(h+5)(h−5)(h+3)=h+4(h−5)(h+3)

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for h:

h+4=0⟹h=−4

$$
\frac{{h}^{2}+9h+20}{{h}^{3}+3{h}^{2}-25h-75}=0.

$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ below, find $\text{E}[Y].$

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals.

| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.25$ | $…$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.25$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ | $…$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ | $1$ |

Therefore, the probability mass function for  $Y$ is given by the following table:

| $y$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.3$ | $0.25$ | $0.45$ |

Finally, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.25+2\cdot 0.45 \\  & =0+0.25+0.9 \\  & =1.15.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{4},$ find $\text{E}[4X+6Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y[{x}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+6Y] & =4\,\text{E}[X]+6\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =4(\frac{3}{4})+6(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =3+8 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}), & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{23}{15},$ find $\text{E}[3X-Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{[{x}^{3}y+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(2{x}^{3}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{[\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(\frac{1}{5}+1-0) \\  & =\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X-Y] & =3\,\text{E}[X]+(-1)\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =3\,(\frac{8}{15})-(\frac{23}{15}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables X and Y below, find E[Y].

f Y=0 Y=1 Y=2

X=1 0.25 0.15 0.2

4.92

EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f(x,y) Y=0 Y=1 Y=2 fX

fY 0.3 0.25 0.45 1

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y[{x}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+6Y] & =4\,\text{E}[X]+6\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =4(\frac{3}{4})+6(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =3+8 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{4},$ find $\text{E}[4X+6Y].$

$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+6Y] & =4\,\text{E}[X]+6\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =4(\frac{3}{4})+6(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =3+8 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Let X and Y be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function f(x,y)={32x2y,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2,0,otherwise. Given that E[X]=34, find E[4X+6Y].

a
72
b
15
c
9
d
32
e
11
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We're given E[X]. So, we first need to compute E[Y].

The marginal density function for Y when 0≤y≤2 is fY(y)=∫−∞∞f(x,y)dx=∫0132x2ydx=12y[x3]01=12y(13−0)=y2.

Therefore, the expected value of Y is E[Y]=∫−∞∞yfY(y)dy=∫01y⋅y2dy=12∫02y2dy=16[y3]02=16(8−0)=43.

Finally, we obtain

E[4X+6Y]=4E[X]+6E[Y]=4(34)+6(43)=3+8=11.

Question 4
?

Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables X and Y below, find E[2X+4Y].

f Y=−2 Y=0 Y=2 Y=4
X=−1 0.05 0.1 0.05 0.1
X=1 0.1 0.05 0.15 0.05
X=3 0.05 0.05 0.15 0.1
a
9.2
b
5.9
c
6.5
d
7.4
e
9.05
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f Y=−2 Y=0 Y=2 Y=4 fX
X=−1 0.05 0.1 0.05 0.1 0.3
X=1 0.1 0.05 0.15 0.05 0.35
X=3 0.05 0.05 0.15 0.1 0.35
fY 0.2 0.2 0.35 0.25 1

Therefore, the probability mass functions for X and Y are given by the following tables:

x −1 1 3
fX(x) 0.3 0.35 0.35

y −2 0 2 4
fY(y) 0.2 0.2 0.35 0.25

Now, we can compute the expected values for X and Y:

E[X]=∑i=1nxifX(xi)=(−1)⋅0.3+1⋅0.35+3⋅0.35=−0.3+0.35+1.05=1.1

E[Y]=∑i=1nyifY(yi)=(−2)⋅0.2+0⋅0.2+2⋅0.35+4⋅0.25=−0.4+0+0.7+1=1.3.

Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain

E[2X+4Y]=2E[X]+4E[Y]=2(1.1)+4(1.3)=2.2+5.2=7.4.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y, & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{4},$ find $\text{E}[4X+6Y].$
question.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y[{x}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+6Y] & =4\,\text{E}[X]+6\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =4(\frac{3}{4})+6(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =3+8 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

The marginal density function for Y when 0≤y≤2 is fY(y)=∫−∞∞f(x,y)dx=∫0132x2ydx=12y[x3]01=12y(13−0)=y2.

We're given $\text{E}[X].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[Y].$

The marginal density function for $Y$ when $0\le y\le 2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y[{x}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}y({1}^{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $Y$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y}(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{y}{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[4X+6Y] & =4\,\text{E}[X]+6\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =4(\frac{3}{4})+6(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =3+8 \\  & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}), & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{23}{15},$ find $\text{E}[3X-Y].$
question.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{[{x}^{3}y+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(2{x}^{3}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{[\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(\frac{1}{5}+1-0) \\  & =\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X-Y] & =3\,\text{E}[X]+(-1)\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =3\,(\frac{8}{15})-(\frac{23}{15}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{[{x}^{3}y+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(2{x}^{3}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{[\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(\frac{1}{5}+1-0) \\  & =\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X-Y] & =3\,\text{E}[X]+(-1)\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =3\,(\frac{8}{15})-(\frac{23}{15}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}), & 0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{23}{15},$ find $\text{E}[3X-Y].$

We're given $\text{E}[Y].$ So, we first need to compute $\text{E}[X].$

The marginal density function for $X$ when $0\le x\le 1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{2}{9}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{9}{[{x}^{3}y+\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}(2{x}^{3}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the  expected value of $X$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{4}{9}({x}^{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{[\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(\frac{1}{5}+1-0) \\  & =\frac{8}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[3X-Y] & =3\,\text{E}[X]+(-1)\,\text{E}[Y] \\  & =3\,(\frac{8}{15})-(\frac{23}{15}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function f(x,y)={29(x3+y3),0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2,0,otherwise. Given that E[Y]=2315, find E[3X−Y].

a
13
b
15
c
415
d
115
e
35
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We're given E[Y]. So, we first need to compute E[X].

The marginal density function for X when 0≤x≤1 is fX(x)=∫−∞∞f(x,y)dy=∫0229(x3+y3)dy=29[x3y+y44]y=0y=2=29(2x3+244−0)=49(x3+2).

Therefore, the expected value of X is E[X]=∫−∞∞xfX(x)dx=∫01x⋅49(x3+2)dx=49∫01(x4+2x)dx=49[x55+x2]01=49(15+1−0)=815.

Finally, we obtain

E[3X−Y]=3E[X]+(−1)E[Y]=3(815)−(2315)=115.

$x$ $-1$ $1$ $3$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.3$ $0.35$ $0.35$

$y$ $-2$ $0$ $2$ $4$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.2$ $0.2$ $0.35$ $0.25$

Now, we can compute the expected values for $X$ and $Y:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\,{f}_{X}({x}_{i}) \\ & =(-1)\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 0.35+3\cdot 0.35 \\ & =-0.3+0.35+1.05 \\ & =1.1\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}\,{f}_{Y}({y}_{i}) \\ & =(-2)\cdot 0.2+0\cdot 0.2+2\cdot 0.35+4\cdot 0.25 \\ & =-0.4+0+0.7+1 \\ & =1.3.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain $$ \begin{aligned}\text{E}[2X+4Y] & =2\text{E}[X]+4\,\text{E}[Y] \\ & =2(1.1)+4(1.3) \\ & =2.2+5.2 \\ & =7.4.\end{aligned} $$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Given the joint probability distribution for two discrete random variables X and Y below, find E[2X+4Y].

f Y=−2 Y=0 Y=2 Y=4
X=−1 0.05 0.1 0.05 0.1
X=1 0.1 0.05 0.15 0.05
X=3 0.05 0.05 0.15 0.1
a
9.2
b
5.9
c
6.5
d
7.4
e
9.05
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the marginal distribution for X corresponds to the row totals, and the marginal distribution for Y corresponds to the column totals.

f Y=−2 Y=0 Y=2 Y=4 fX
X=−1 0.05 0.1 0.05 0.1 0.3
X=1 0.1 0.05 0.15 0.05 0.35
X=3 0.05 0.05 0.15 0.1 0.35
fY 0.2 0.2 0.35 0.25 1

Therefore, the probability mass functions for X and Y are given by the following tables:

x −1 1 3
fX(x) 0.3 0.35 0.35

y −2 0 2 4
fY(y) 0.2 0.2 0.35 0.25

Now, we can compute the expected values for X and Y:

E[X]=∑i=1nxifX(xi)=(−1)⋅0.3+1⋅0.35+3⋅0.35=−0.3+0.35+1.05=1.1

E[Y]=∑i=1nyifY(yi)=(−2)⋅0.2+0⋅0.2+2⋅0.35+4⋅0.25=−0.4+0+0.7+1=1.3.

Finally, using the properties of expectation, we obtain

E[2X+4Y]=2E[X]+4E[Y]=2(1.1)+4(1.3)=2.2+5.2=7.4.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The function $x(t)$ models the number of meters traveled by a car, $t$ seconds after it sets off on a journey. What is the best interpretation of ${x}^{′}(30)=10?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function ${x}^{′}(t)$ represents the rate at which the number of meters is changing at the moment $t$ seconds after starting its journey.

Therefore, ${x}^{′}(30)=10$ means:

$\,$ *$30$ seconds after the start of the journey, the distance traveled increased at a rate of $10$ meters per second*

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The birth rate of crocodiles in a river is modeled by $B(t)=6\cdot {e}^{0.25t}$ crocodiles per year, while the rate of death is modeled by $D(t)=4\cdot {e}^{0.25t}$ crocodiles per year, where $t$ represents the number of years since the year $2000.$  

What was the rate of change of the crocodile population in $2012?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the crocodile population $t$ years since $2000$ is equal to the birth rate minus the death rate, that is

$$
B(t)-D(t).
$$

Since $2012$ is $12$ years after $2000$, we have $t=12.$ Substituting $t=12,$ the rate of change of the crocodile population in the river  in $2012$ was

$$
\begin{aligned}B(12)-D(12) & =6\cdot {e}^{0.25(12)}-4\cdot {e}^{0.25(12)} \\  & =6{e}^{3}-4{e}^{3} \\  & =2{e}^{3} \\  & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of the crocodile population in the river in $2012$ is approximately $40$ crocodiles per year.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: The electrical resistivity of a copper wire varies with the temperature. The function $R(T)$ gives the resistivity of a wire at a temperature of $T$ degrees Celsius. What is the best interpretation of ${R}^{′}(10)=-0.01?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function ${R}^{′}(T)$ represents the rate at which the resistivity of the wire is decreasing at $T$ degrees Celsius.

Therefore, since it is negative, ${R}^{′}(10)=-0.01$ means:

$\,$ *At $10$ degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases at a rate of $0.01$ units per degree.*

question.html:
Question 1
?

The function x(t) models the number of meters traveled by a car, t seconds after it sets off on a journey. What is the best interpretation of x′(30)=10?

a
30 seconds after the start of the journey, the distance traveled decreased at a rate of 10 meters per second
b
The distance traveled increased by 10 meters during the first 30 seconds
c
30 seconds after the start of the journey, the distance traveled increased at a rate of 10 meters per second
d
The distance traveled increased at a constant rate of 3 meters per second
e
30 seconds after the start of the journey, the car traveled 10 meters.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The function x′(t) represents the rate at which the number of meters is changing at the moment t seconds after starting its journey.

Therefore, x′(30)=10 means:

30 seconds after the start of the journey, the distance traveled increased at a rate of 10 meters per second

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the crocodile population $t$ years since $2000$ is equal to the birth rate minus the death rate, that is

$$
B(t)-D(t).
$$

Since $2012$ is $12$ years after $2000$, we have $t=12.$ Substituting $t=12,$ the rate of change of the crocodile population in the river  in $2012$ was

$$
\begin{aligned}B(12)-D(12) & =6\cdot {e}^{0.25(12)}-4\cdot {e}^{0.25(12)} \\  & =6{e}^{3}-4{e}^{3} \\  & =2{e}^{3} \\  & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of the crocodile population in the river in $2012$ is approximately $40$ crocodiles per year.

At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The birth rate of crocodiles in a river is modeled by $B(t)=6\cdot {e}^{0.25t}$ crocodiles per year, while the rate of death is modeled by $D(t)=4\cdot {e}^{0.25t}$ crocodiles per year, where $t$ represents the number of years since the year $2000.$  

What was the rate of change of the crocodile population in $2012?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.
question.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the crocodile population $t$ years since $2000$ is equal to the birth rate minus the death rate, that is

$$
B(t)-D(t).
$$

Since $2012$ is $12$ years after $2000$, we have $t=12.$ Substituting $t=12,$ the rate of change of the crocodile population in the river  in $2012$ was

$$
\begin{aligned}B(12)-D(12) & =6\cdot {e}^{0.25(12)}-4\cdot {e}^{0.25(12)} \\  & =6{e}^{3}-4{e}^{3} \\  & =2{e}^{3} \\  & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of the crocodile population in the river in $2012$ is approximately $40$ crocodiles per year.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: The electrical resistivity of a copper wire varies with the temperature. The function $R(T)$ gives the resistivity of a wire at a temperature of $T$ degrees Celsius. What is the best interpretation of ${R}^{′}(10)=-0.01?$

question.html:
Question 3
?

The electrical resistivity of a copper wire varies with the temperature. The function R(T) gives the resistivity of a wire at a temperature of T degrees Celsius. What is the best interpretation of R′(10)=−0.01?

a
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire increases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree
b
For each interval of 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases by 0.01 units
c
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire is 0.01 units
d
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire is 0.01 units less than its value at 0∘
e
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function R′(T) represents the rate at which the resistivity of the wire is decreasing at T degrees Celsius.

Therefore, since it is negative, R′(10)=−0.01 means:

At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree.

question.html:
Question 3
?

The electrical resistivity of a copper wire varies with the temperature. The function R(T) gives the resistivity of a wire at a temperature of T degrees Celsius. What is the best interpretation of R′(10)=−0.01?

a
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire increases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree
b
For each interval of 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases by 0.01 units
c
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire is 0.01 units
d
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire is 0.01 units less than its value at 0∘
e
At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function R′(T) represents the rate at which the resistivity of the wire is decreasing at T degrees Celsius.

Therefore, since it is negative, R′(10)=−0.01 means:

At 10 degrees Celsius, the resistivity of the wire decreases at a rate of 0.01 units per degree.

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199494/assets/f5b33723509f58055f0ded0c575ea097cc90ff05fcfc72fc3270553248de0f2b.png)

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-3.$ Therefore, $c=-3.$

questions.raw_html:

The graph above shows the curve y=(18)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199494/assets/c091fc5d742ddca3090725974f00ff7da77b1530d601bb82e288518b27970b0a.png)

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.5.$ Therefore, $c=2.5.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which of the following is the graph of $y=2{(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}+3?$
questions.worked_solution:
We start with plotting the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199494/assets/75bb797ddbea41de97c1c4ba52e142342bfffb4f9b2b9b82111ebc94abf55446.png)

Next, we plot the graph of $y=2{(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}.$ To do this, we scale the graph above by a factor of $2.$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,2)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199494/assets/d68957038bfad7dfb4547d69abd178b087dde6c0f7c8ba95aa0fcd7547ccebe6.png)

Finally, we plot the graph of $y=2{(\frac{1}{7})}^{x}+3.$ To do this, we shift the above graph $3$ units up. The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,2)$ to $(0,5)$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199494/assets/fb918b3042ca95c9401f2938258b7f13c909a87d18448c6e36c410a3d092dd94.png)

question.html:
Question 1
?

The graph above shows the curve y=(18)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

a
y=(18)x−3
b
y=(18)x−2
c
y=(18)x+3
d
y=(18)x+2
e
y=(18)x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The horizontal asymptote of y=(18)x is y=0.

The vertical translation y=(18)x+c shifts the asymptote to y=c.

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is y=−3. Therefore, c=−3.

Question 2
?

The graph above shows the curve y=(19)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

a
y=(19)x+3.5
b
y=(19)x−2.5
c
y=(19)x+2.5
d
y=(19)x+1.5
e
y=(19)x−3.5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The horizontal asymptote of y=(19)x is y=0.

The vertical translation y=(19)x+c shifts the asymptote to y=c.

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is y=2.5. Therefore, c=2.5.

question.html:
Question 1
?

The graph above shows the curve y=(18)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

a
y=(18)x−3
b
y=(18)x−2
c
y=(18)x+3
d
y=(18)x+2
e
y=(18)x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The horizontal asymptote of y=(18)x is y=0.

The vertical translation y=(18)x+c shifts the asymptote to y=c.

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is y=−3. Therefore, c=−3.

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
question.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-3.$ Therefore, $c=-3.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The graph above shows the curve y=(18)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

a
y=(18)x−3
b
y=(18)x−2
c
y=(18)x+3
d
y=(18)x+2
e
y=(18)x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The horizontal asymptote of y=(18)x is y=0.

The vertical translation y=(18)x+c shifts the asymptote to y=c.

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is y=−3. Therefore, c=−3.

solution.reasoning: The horizontal asymptote is y=-3. Since (1/8)^x approaches 0 as x increases, the asymptote is y=c, so c=-3 and y=(1/8)^x-3, option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade verifies its key.

Question 1
?

The graph above shows the curve y=(18)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

a
y=(18)x−3
b
y=(18)x−2
c
y=(18)x+3
d
y=(18)x+2
e
y=(18)x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The horizontal asymptote of y=(18)x is y=0.

The vertical translation y=(18)x+c shifts the asymptote to y=c.

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is y=−3. Therefore, c=−3.

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
question.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{9})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.5.$ Therefore, $c=2.5.$

Question 2
?

The graph above shows the curve y=(19)x+c. Determine the value of c and find the equation of the curve.

a
y=(19)x+3.5
b
y=(19)x−2.5
c
y=(19)x+2.5
d
y=(19)x+1.5
e
y=(19)x−3.5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The horizontal asymptote of y=(19)x is y=0.

The vertical translation y=(19)x+c shifts the asymptote to y=c.

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is y=2.5. Therefore, c=2.5.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $y=4\operatorname{coth}⁡x-\operatorname{csch}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{coth}⁡x-\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =4(-{csch}^{2}⁡x)-(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-4{csch}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{csch}⁡x(-4\operatorname{csch}⁡x+\operatorname{coth}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $y=\operatorname{sech}⁡x-2\operatorname{csch}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sech}⁡x-2\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-2(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+2\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=4\operatorname{sech}⁡3x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=4\operatorname{sech}⁡g,\,g=3x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=-4\operatorname{sech}⁡g\operatorname{tanh}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=3.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-4\operatorname{sech}⁡g\operatorname{tanh}⁡g\cdot 3 \\  & =-12\operatorname{sech}⁡g\operatorname{tanh}⁡g \\  & =-12\operatorname{sech}⁡3x\operatorname{tanh}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡{x}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=-\operatorname{csch}⁡g,\,g={x}^{2}
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=2x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡{x}^{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=2{sech}^{2}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=2{g}^{2},\,g=\operatorname{sech}⁡x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4g(-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) \\  & =4(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)(-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) \\  & =-4{sech}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=-2\operatorname{csch}⁡(1-4x).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=-2\operatorname{csch}⁡g,\,g=1-4x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=2\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g\cdot (-4) \\  & =-8\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g \\  & =-8\operatorname{csch}⁡(1-4x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(1-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=\operatorname{coth}⁡({x}^{2}-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=\operatorname{coth}⁡g,\,g={x}^{2}-1
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=-{csch}^{2}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=2x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-{csch}^{2}⁡g\cdot 2x \\  & =-2x{csch}^{2}⁡g \\  & =-2x{csch}^{2}⁡({x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
$$

If $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{csch}⁡4x,$ then ${f}^{′}(x)=2x\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\cdot g(x).$ What is $g(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{csch}⁡4x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({x}^{2})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{csch}⁡4x+{x}^{2}\cdot {(\operatorname{csch}⁡4x)}^{′} \\  & =2x\cdot \operatorname{csch}⁡4x+{x}^{2}\cdot (-4\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x) \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡4x-4{x}^{2}\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\cdot {{(1-2x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x)}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=1-2x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=-3x{csch}^{2}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=-3x$ and $v(x)={csch}^{2}⁡x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(-3x)}^{′}\cdot {csch}^{2}⁡x+(-3x)\cdot {({csch}^{2}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =-3\cdot {csch}^{2}⁡x-3x\cdot (2\operatorname{csch}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-3{csch}^{2}⁡x+6x{csch}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x \\  & =3{csch}^{2}⁡x(2x\operatorname{coth}⁡x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=2{x}^{3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=2{x}^{3}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{coth}⁡x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(2{x}^{3})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡x+2{x}^{3}\cdot {(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =6{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡x+2{x}^{3}\cdot (-{csch}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =6{x}^{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x-2{x}^{3}{csch}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2{x}^{2}(3\operatorname{coth}⁡x-x{csch}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=2x\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=2x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(2x)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}+2x\cdot {(\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2})}^{′} \\  & =2\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}+2x\cdot (-2x{csch}^{2}⁡{x}^{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}{csch}^{2}⁡{x}^{2} \\  & =2(\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}-2{x}^{2}{csch}^{2}⁡{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=x\operatorname{sech}⁡3x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{sech}⁡3x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sech}⁡3x+x\cdot (\operatorname{sech}⁡3x)^{′} \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sech}⁡3x+x\cdot (-3\operatorname{sech}⁡3x\cdot \operatorname{tanh}⁡3x) \\  & =\operatorname{sech}⁡3x-3x\operatorname{sech}⁡3x\operatorname{tanh}⁡3x \\  & =\operatorname{sech}⁡3x(1-3x\operatorname{tanh}⁡3x)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

If $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{csch}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x},$ then ${f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{g(x)}{x{ln}^{2}⁡x}.$ What is $g(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{x})}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{\overset{g(x)}{\overset{⏞}{\operatorname{csch}⁡x(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x+1)}}}{x{ln}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{csch}⁡x(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x+1).$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{csch}⁡x}{2{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ and $v(x)=2{x}^{2}.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}\cdot 2{x}^{2}-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\cdot (2{x}^{2})^{′}}{(2{x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x-4x\operatorname{csch}⁡x}{4{x}^{4}} \\  & =-\frac{2x\operatorname{csch}⁡x(x\operatorname{coth}⁡x+2)}{4{x}^{4}} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{csch}⁡x(x\operatorname{coth}⁡x+2)}{2{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\cdot {(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{\overset{g(x)}{\overset{⏞}{\operatorname{sech}⁡x(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}}}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{sech}⁡x(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x).$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{\operatorname{sech}⁡2x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{sech}⁡2x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{({x}^{2})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sech}⁡2x-{x}^{2}\cdot {(\operatorname{sech}⁡2x)}^{′}}{{(\operatorname{sech}⁡2x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\operatorname{sech}⁡2x-{x}^{2}(-2\operatorname{sech}⁡2x\operatorname{tanh}⁡2x)}{{sech}^{2}⁡2x} \\  & =\frac{2x\operatorname{sech}⁡2x(1+x\operatorname{tanh}⁡2x)}{{sech}^{2}⁡2x} \\  & =\frac{2x(1+x\operatorname{tanh}⁡2x)}{\operatorname{sech}⁡2x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 20
questions.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{csch}⁡x}{{3}^{x}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $f(x)$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=\operatorname{csch}⁡x$ and $v(x)={3}^{x}.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)}^{′}\cdot {3}^{x}-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\cdot {({3}^{x})}^{′}}{{({3}^{x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x)\cdot {3}^{x}-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\cdot ({3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}{{3}^{2x}} \\  & =-\frac{{3}^{x}\operatorname{csch}⁡x(\operatorname{coth}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}{{3}^{2x}} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{csch}⁡x(\operatorname{coth}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡3)}{{3}^{x}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{coth}⁡x-\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =4(-{csch}^{2}⁡x)-(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-4{csch}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{csch}⁡x(-4\operatorname{csch}⁡x+\operatorname{coth}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Find the derivative of y=4coth⁡x−csch⁡x.

a
sech⁡x(4sech⁡x−coth⁡x)
b
csch⁡x(−4csch⁡x+coth⁡x)
c
−csch⁡x(4csch⁡x+coth⁡x)
d
4csch2⁡x−coth⁡x
e
−4csch2⁡x+coth⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

(sech⁡x)′=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x,(csch⁡x)′=−csch⁡xcoth⁡x,(coth⁡x)′=−csch2⁡x

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

dydx=ddx(4coth⁡x−csch⁡x)=4ddx(coth⁡x)−ddx(csch⁡x)=4(−csch2⁡x)−(−csch⁡xcoth⁡x)=−4csch2⁡x+csch⁡xcoth⁡x=csch⁡x(−4csch⁡x+coth⁡x).
question.knowledge_point: Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =6(-{csch}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-6{csch}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Find the derivative of y=−3csch⁡x.

a
 −3csch2⁡x
b
 3sech⁡xtanh⁡x
c
 3sech⁡x
d
 3csch⁡xcoth⁡x
e
 −3csch⁡xcoth⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

(sech⁡x)′=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x,(csch⁡x)′=−csch⁡xcoth⁡x,(coth⁡x)′=−csch2⁡x

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

dydx=ddx(−3csch⁡x)=−3ddx(csch⁡x)=−3(−csch⁡xcoth⁡x)=3csch⁡xcoth⁡x.
question.knowledge_point: Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{csch}⁡x-\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-3\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x-(-{csch}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{csch}⁡x(\operatorname{csch}⁡x-3\operatorname{coth}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the derivative of y=3csch⁡x−coth⁡x.

a
csch⁡x(3csch⁡x+coth⁡x)
b
3csch⁡xcoth⁡x−sech2⁡x
c
coth⁡x(csch⁡x−3coth⁡x)
d
csch⁡xcoth⁡x+3csch2⁡x
e
csch⁡x(csch⁡x−3coth⁡x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

(sech⁡x)′=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x,(csch⁡x)′=−csch⁡xcoth⁡x,(coth⁡x)′=−csch2⁡x

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

dydx=ddx(3csch⁡x−coth⁡x)=3ddx(csch⁡x)−ddx(coth⁡x)=−3csch⁡xcoth⁡x−(−csch2⁡x)=csch⁡x(csch⁡x−3coth⁡x).

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Basic Derivatives of the Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sech}⁡x-2\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-2(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+2\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

$$
(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{csch}⁡x)^{′}=-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x,\,(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)^{′}=-{csch}^{2}⁡x
$$

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sech}⁡x-2\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{csch}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x-2(-\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+2\operatorname{csch}⁡x\operatorname{coth}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Find the derivative of y=sech⁡x−2csch⁡x.

a
 sech⁡x(tanh⁡x+2csch⁡x)
b
sech⁡x(−tanh⁡x−2sech⁡x)
c
−sech⁡xtanh⁡x+2csch⁡xcoth⁡x
d
−sech⁡xtanh⁡x+2csch2⁡xcoth⁡x
e
sech⁡xtanh⁡x−2csch2⁡xcoth⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we recall the results for the derivatives of the basic reciprocal hyperbolic functions:

(sech⁡x)′=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x,(csch⁡x)′=−csch⁡xcoth⁡x,(coth⁡x)′=−csch2⁡x

Differentiating the given function using these results, we get

dydx=ddx(sech⁡x−2csch⁡x)=ddx(sech⁡x)−2ddx(csch⁡x)=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x−2(−csch⁡xcoth⁡x)=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x+2csch⁡xcoth⁡x.

Find the derivative of f(x)=4sech⁡3x.

a
 8sech⁡3xtanh⁡3x
b
 12csch⁡3xtanh⁡3x

 −12sech⁡3xtanh⁡3x

 −12tanh2⁡3x
e
 −4csch2⁡3x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express f(x) as a composite function:

f=4sech⁡g,g=3x

The chain rule states that

dfdx=dfdg⋅dgdx.

Differentiating, we have

dfdg=−4sech⁡gtanh⁡g,

and

dgdx=3.

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for g gives

dfdx=−4sech⁡gtanh⁡g⋅3=−12sech⁡gtanh⁡g=−12sech⁡3xtanh⁡3x.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=-\operatorname{csch}⁡g,\,g={x}^{2}
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=2x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g\cdot 2x \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡{x}^{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Find the derivative of f(x)=−csch⁡x2.

a
2xcoth2⁡x2
b
csch⁡2xcoth⁡2x
c
2xcsch⁡x2coth⁡x2
d
−2xsech⁡x2coth⁡x2
e
x2csch⁡x2coth⁡x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we express f(x) as a composite function:

f=−csch⁡g,g=x2

The chain rule states that

dfdx=dfdg⋅dgdx.

Differentiating, we have

dfdg=csch⁡gcoth⁡g,

and

dgdx=2x.

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for g gives

dfdx=csch⁡gcoth⁡g⋅2x=2xcsch⁡gcoth⁡g=2xcsch⁡x2coth⁡x2.
question.knowledge_point: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Chain Rule

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Chain Rule
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=2{g}^{2},\,g=\operatorname{sech}⁡x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4g(-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) \\  & =4(\operatorname{sech}⁡x)(-\operatorname{sech}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x) \\  & =-4{sech}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tanh}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

a
 −4sech2⁡xtanh⁡x
b
 4sech⁡xtanh⁡x
c
 4sech⁡xtanh2⁡x
d
2sech⁡x
e
−2sech⁡xtanh2⁡x
Submit
Correct

First, we express f(x) as a composite function:

f=2g2,g=sech⁡x

The chain rule states that

dfdx=dfdg⋅dgdx.

Differentiating, we have

dfdg=4g,

dgdx=−sech⁡xtanh⁡x.

dfdx=4g(−sech⁡xtanh⁡x)=4(sech⁡x)(−sech⁡xtanh⁡x)=−4sech2⁡xtanh⁡x.

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Chain Rule
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=-2\operatorname{csch}⁡g,\,g=1-4x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=2\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g\cdot (-4) \\  & =-8\operatorname{csch}⁡g\operatorname{coth}⁡g \\  & =-8\operatorname{csch}⁡(1-4x)\operatorname{coth}⁡(1-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Find the derivative of f(x)=−2csch⁡(1−4x).

a
−8sech⁡(1−4x)coth⁡(1−4x)
b
−8csch⁡(1−4x)coth⁡(1−4x)
c
4sech⁡(1−4x)coth⁡(1−4x)
d
2csch⁡(1−4x)coth⁡(1−4x)
e
−4csch⁡(1−4x)tanh⁡(1−4x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we express f(x) as a composite function:

f=−2csch⁡g,g=1−4x

The chain rule states that dfdx=dfdg⋅dgdx.

Differentiating, we have dfdg=2csch⁡gcoth⁡g,

and dgdx=−4.

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for g gives

dfdx=2csch⁡gcoth⁡g⋅(−4)=−8csch⁡gcoth⁡g=−8csch⁡(1−4x)coth⁡(1−4x).
question.knowledge_point: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Chain Rule

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Chain Rule
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=\operatorname{coth}⁡g,\,g={x}^{2}-1
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=-{csch}^{2}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=2x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-{csch}^{2}⁡g\cdot 2x \\  & =-2x{csch}^{2}⁡g \\  & =-2x{csch}^{2}⁡({x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=\operatorname{coth}⁡({x}^{2}-1).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f=\operatorname{coth}⁡g,\,g={x}^{2}-1
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=-{csch}^{2}⁡g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=2x.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-{csch}^{2}⁡g\cdot 2x \\  & =-2x{csch}^{2}⁡g \\  & =-2x{csch}^{2}⁡({x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find the derivative of f(x)=coth⁡(x2−1).

a
−x3csch2⁡2x
b
−2xcsch⁡(x2−1)coth⁡(x2−1)
c
−xcsch2⁡2x
d
−2xcsch2⁡(x2−1)
e
2xsech2⁡(x2−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express f(x) as a composite function: f=coth⁡g,g=x2−1

The chain rule states that dfdx=dfdg⋅dgdx.

Differentiating, we have dfdg=−csch2⁡g,

and dgdx=2x.

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for g gives dfdx=−csch2⁡g⋅2x=−2xcsch2⁡g=−2xcsch2⁡(x2−1).

observed_steps.name: Question 11
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Product Rule
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{csch}⁡4x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({x}^{2})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{csch}⁡4x+{x}^{2}\cdot {(\operatorname{csch}⁡4x)}^{′} \\  & =2x\cdot \operatorname{csch}⁡4x+{x}^{2}\cdot (-4\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x) \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡4x-4{x}^{2}\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x \\  & =2x\operatorname{csch}⁡4x\cdot {{(1-2x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x)}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=1-2x\operatorname{coth}⁡4x.$

question.html:
Question 11
?

If f(x)=x2csch⁡4x, then f′(x)=2xcsch⁡4x⋅g(x). What is g(x)?

a
 1+xcoth⁡4x
b
2−xcoth⁡4x
c
1−2xtanh⁡4x
d
 1−2xcoth⁡4x
e
 2+xcsch⁡4x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Here, we have the product of two functions u(x)=x2 and v(x)=csch⁡4x. So, we apply the product rule:

f′(x)=(x2)′⋅csch⁡4x+x2⋅(csch⁡4x)′=2x⋅csch⁡4x+x2⋅(−4csch⁡4xcoth⁡4x)=2xcsch⁡4x−4x2csch⁡4xcoth⁡4x=2xcsch⁡4x⋅(1−2xcoth⁡4x)⏟g(x)

Therefore, g(x)=1−2xcoth⁡4x.

question.html:
Question 12
?

Find the derivative of f(x)=−3xcsch2⁡x.

a
3csch2⁡x(2xcoth⁡x−1)
b
−3csch2⁡x(2xcoth⁡x+1)
c
3csch⁡x(2xcoth2⁡x−1)
d
−3csch2⁡x(2xcoth2⁡x+1)
e
−3csch⁡x(csch⁡x+2xcoth2⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we have the product of two functions u(x)=−3x and v(x)=csch2⁡x. So, we apply the product rule:

f′(x)=(−3x)′⋅csch2⁡x+(−3x)⋅(csch2⁡x)′=−3⋅csch2⁡x−3x⋅(2csch⁡x)⋅(−csch⁡xcoth⁡x)=−3csch2⁡x+6xcsch2⁡xcoth⁡x=3csch2⁡x(2xcoth⁡x−1)
question.knowledge_point: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Product Rule

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Differentiating Reciprocal Hyperbolic Functions Using the Product Rule
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=2{x}^{3}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{coth}⁡x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(2{x}^{3})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡x+2{x}^{3}\cdot {(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =6{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡x+2{x}^{3}\cdot (-{csch}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =6{x}^{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x-2{x}^{3}{csch}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2{x}^{2}(3\operatorname{coth}⁡x-x{csch}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
$$

Find the derivative of $f(x)=2{x}^{3}\operatorname{coth}⁡x.$
question.worked_solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=2{x}^{3}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{coth}⁡x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(2{x}^{3})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡x+2{x}^{3}\cdot {(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =6{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{coth}⁡x+2{x}^{3}\cdot (-{csch}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =6{x}^{2}\operatorname{coth}⁡x-2{x}^{3}{csch}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2{x}^{2}(3\operatorname{coth}⁡x-x{csch}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$
