question.problem:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(6,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=4,\,{x}_{2}=3,\,{x}_{3}=5.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$

*Hint: The probability mass function for a binomial random variable is given by*

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{6-x},\,x=0,1,…,6.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=3$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=6$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{6-x},\,x=0,1,…,6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{6-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(6-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{4})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{5}) \\  & =15\cdot 20\cdot 6 \\  & =1\,800,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=4+3+5=12.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\,800)+12\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(6\cdot 3-12)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1\,800+12\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +6\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=1\,800+12+6=1\,818.
$$

Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=3$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{3-x},\,x=0,1,2,3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{3-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{3-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(3-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(3-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{4}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{5}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1}) \\  & =3\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 3\cdot 3 \\  & =81,\end{aligned}

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Suppose X1,X2,…,X5 is an I.I.D random sample with Xi∼B(3,θ) with unknown probability of success θ. You're given the particular sample x1=2,x2=1,x3=3,x4=1,x5=1. The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by l(θ)=ln⁡a+bln⁡θ+cln⁡(1−θ).

Find the value of a+b+c.

a
96
b
92
c
88
d
104
e
112
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X1,X2,…,Xn are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function f(x;θ), where θ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample x1,x2,…,xn is l(θ)=ln⁡L(θ)=ln⁡(∏i=1nf(xi,θ))=∑i=1nln⁡(f(xi,θ)).

In our case, we are given a sample of n=5 independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success θ and N=3 as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is f(x,θ)=(Nx)θx(1−θ)N−x,x=0,1,…,N=(3x)θx(1−θ)3−x,x=0,1,2,3.

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows: l(θ)=∑i=1nln⁡((3xi)θxi(1−θ)3−xi)=∑i=1nln⁡(3xi)+ln⁡(θxi)+ln⁡((1−θ)3−xi)=∑i=1nln⁡(3xi)+∑i=1nxiln⁡θ+∑i=1n(3−xi)ln⁡(1−θ)=∑i=1nln⁡(3xi)+ln⁡θ∑i=1nxi+ln⁡(1−θ)∑i=1n(3−xi)=∑i=1nln⁡(3xi)+Sln⁡θ+(3n−S)ln⁡(1−θ) where S=∑i=1nxi.

Now, note that ∑i=1nln⁡(3xi)=ln⁡(3x1)+ln⁡(3x2)+ln⁡(3x3)+ln⁡(3x4)+ln⁡(3x5)=ln⁡(∏i=1n(3xi)).

So, our expression for l(θ) becomes l(θ)=ln⁡(∏i=1n(3xi))+Sln⁡θ+(3n−S)ln⁡(1−θ).

Now, using the sample data with n=5, we have ∏i=1n(3xi)=(32)⋅(31)⋅(33)⋅(31)⋅(31)=3⋅3⋅1⋅3⋅3=81,

and S=2+1+3+1+1=8.

Substituting the above values into our expression for l(θ), we get l(θ)=ln⁡(81)+8ln⁡θ+(3⋅5−8)ln⁡(1−θ)=ln⁡(81)+8ln⁡θ+7ln⁡(1−θ).

Finally, a+b+c=81+8+7=96.

solution.reasoning: The likelihood is L(\theta)=\binom{3}{2}\binom{3}{1}\binom{3}{3}\binom{3}{1}\binom{3}{1}\theta^{2+1+3+1+1}(1-\theta)^{1+2+0+2+2}=81\theta^8(1-\theta)^7. Thus a=81, b=8 and c=7, giving a+b+c=96. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem:
Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼B(3,\theta )$ with unknown probability of success $\theta .$ You're given the particular sample 

$$
{x}_{1}=2,\,{x}_{2}=1,\,{x}_{3}=3,\,{x}_{4}=1,\,{x}_{5}=1.
$$

The log-likelihood function of the sample is given by

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡a+b\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +c\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed discrete random variables with probability mass function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the log-likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡L(\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i},\theta )) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(f({x}_{i},\theta )).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=5$ independent binomial random variables with an unknown probability of success $\theta $ and $N=3$ as the number of trials. Therefore, the probability mass function is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,\theta ) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{N}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{N-x},\,x=0,1,…,N \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{x}){\theta }^{x}(1-\theta )^{3-x},\,x=0,1,2,3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the log-likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡((\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}){\theta }^{{x}_{i}}(1-\theta )^{3-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({\theta }^{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-\theta )^{3-{x}_{i}}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(3-{x}_{i})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta {\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ){\sum }_{i=1}^{n}(3-{x}_{i}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta )\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}.$

Now, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{1}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{2}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{3}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{4}})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{5}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, our expression for $l(\theta )$ becomes

$$
l(\theta )=\operatorname{ln}⁡({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}))+S\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3n-S)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).
$$

Now, using the sample data with $n=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{{x}_{i}}) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{2})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{3})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1})\cdot (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1}) \\  & =3\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 3\cdot 3 \\  & =81,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
S=2+1+3+1+1=8.
$$

Substituting the above values into our expression for $l(\theta )$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}l(\theta ) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(81)+8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +(3\cdot 5-8)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(81)+8\operatorname{ln}⁡\theta +7\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=81+8+7=96.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What is the value of $15{\text{i}}^{4}+15{\text{i}}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the first few powers of $\text{i},$ where $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{0} & =1 \\ {\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot \text{i}=(-1)\cdot \text{i}=-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot {\text{i}}^{2}=(-1)\cdot (-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}15{\text{i}}^{4}+15{\text{i}}^{2}=15(1)+15(-1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: What is the value of ${\text{i}}^{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the first few powers of $\text{i},$ where $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{0} & =1 \\ {\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot \text{i}=(-1)\cdot \text{i}=-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot {\text{i}}^{2}=(-1)\cdot (-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, using the laws of exponents, we can write

$$
8{\text{i}}^{-1}=\frac{8}{\text{i}}.
$$

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $\text{i},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{\text{i}}=\frac{8}{\text{i}}\cdot \frac{\text{i}}{\text{i}}=\frac{8\text{i}}{{\text{i}}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now recall that ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{8\text{i}}{{\text{i}}^{2}}=\frac{8\text{i}}{(-1)}=\frac{8}{(-1)}\cdot \text{i}=-8\text{i}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: What is the value of $4\textrm{i}^3?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's recall the first few powers of $\textrm{i},$ where $\textrm{i} = \sqrt{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{0} & =1 \\ {\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot \text{i}=(-1)\cdot \text{i}=-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot {\text{i}}^{2}=(-1)\cdot (-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\text{i}}^{3} & =4\cdot (-\text{i})=-4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Raising i to a Positive Integer Power Using the Cyclic Property
canonical_examples.problem: Simplify $\textrm{i}^{15}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the value of $\textrm{i}$ to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=15.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
15\div 4 = 3\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{3}.
$$

So the remainder is $\color{blue}3.$ Therefore,

$$
\textrm{i}^{15} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{3}} = -\textrm{i}.
$$

tutorials.name: The Cyclic Nature of Powers of i
tutorials.problem:
Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of $\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & =-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

At the fourth power, we return to the value of $1,$ which can also be written as $\textrm{i}^0 = 1.$ This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199584/assets/5e3f3a42dd591daf109e474eec99e446706e0d8e46f1252540839cd50d957463.png)

So, for $\textrm{i}^5$ through $\textrm{i}^8,$ the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that $\textrm{i}^4 = 1,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 .
	}
$$

Similarly, for $\textrm{i}^9$ through to $\textrm{i}^{12},$ the pattern repeats again:

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 
	}
$$

Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of $\textrm{i},$ we *divide the power by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder*.

Let's see this idea in action.

tutorial.name: The Cyclic Nature of Powers of i
tutorial.problem:
Let's remind ourselves of the first few powers of $\textrm{i}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & =-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

At the fourth power, we return to the value of $1,$ which can also be written as $\textrm{i}^0 = 1.$ This means that if we continue to increase the powers, we would cycle through the same four values once again, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14199584/assets/5e3f3a42dd591daf109e474eec99e446706e0d8e46f1252540839cd50d957463.png)

So, for $\textrm{i}^5$ through $\textrm{i}^8,$ the exact same pattern repeats. Remembering that $\textrm{i}^4 = 1,$ we have

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^5&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^6&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^7&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^8&=\textrm{i}^4 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 .
	}
$$

Similarly, for $\textrm{i}^9$ through to $\textrm{i}^{12},$ the pattern repeats again:

$$
\eqalign{
		\textrm{i}^9&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i} &= \textrm{i}\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{10}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^2 &=-1\[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{11}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^3 &= -\textrm{i} \[5pt]
		\textrm{i}^{12}&=(\textrm{i}^4)^2 \cdot \textrm{i}^4 &= 1 
	}
$$

Therefore, to simplify a higher integer power of $\textrm{i},$ we *divide the power by $4$ and raise $\textrm{i}$ to the remainder*.

Let's see this idea in action.

$$
15\div 4 = 3\,\textrm{R} \color{blue}{3}.
$$

So the remainder is $\color{blue}3.$ Therefore,

$$
\textrm{i}^{15} = \textrm{i}^{\color{blue}{3}} = -\textrm{i}.
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: What is the value of $15{\text{i}}^{4}+15{\text{i}}^{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
Let's recall the first few powers of $\text{i},$ where $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{i}}^{0} & =1 \\ {\text{i}}^{1} & =\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{2} & =-1 \\ {\text{i}}^{3} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot \text{i}=(-1)\cdot \text{i}=-\text{i} \\ {\text{i}}^{4} & ={\text{i}}^{2}\cdot {\text{i}}^{2}=(-1)\cdot (-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}15{\text{i}}^{4}+15{\text{i}}^{2}=15(1)+15(-1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Simplify ${\text{i}}^{27}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the value of $\text{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4,$ and raise $\text{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=27.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
27÷4=6\,\text{R}3.
$$

So the remainder is $3.$ Therefore,

$$
{\text{i}}^{27}={\text{i}}^{3}=-\text{i}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Raising i to a Positive Integer Power Using the Cyclic Property
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the value of $\text{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4,$ and raise $\text{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=27.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
27÷4=6\,\text{R}3.
$$

So the remainder is $3.$ Therefore,

$$
{\text{i}}^{27}={\text{i}}^{3}=-\text{i}.
$$

To find the value of i raised to some positive integer power n, we divide n by 4, and raise i to the remainder.

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
Using the power law for exponents, we have

$$
{({\text{i}}^{3})}^{10}={\text{i}}^{3\cdot 10}={\text{i}}^{30}.
$$

To find the value of $\text{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4,$ and raise $\text{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=30.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
30÷4=7\,\text{R}2.
$$

So the remainder is $2.$ Therefore,

$$
{\text{i}}^{30}={\text{i}}^{2}=-1.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating an Expression Involving Powers of i Using the Laws of Exponents
last_observation.worked_solution:
Using the power law for exponents, we have

$$
{a}^{3}={({\text{i}}^{5})}^{3}={\text{i}}^{5\cdot 3}={\text{i}}^{15}.
$$

To find the value of $\text{i}$ raised to some positive integer power $n$, we divide $n$ by $4,$ and raise $\text{i}$ to the remainder.

In our case, we have $n=15.$ Dividing the power by $4,$ we get

$$
15÷4=3\,\text{R}3.
$$

So the remainder is $3.$ Therefore,

$$
{\text{i}}^{15}={\text{i}}^{3}=-\text{i}.
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.worked_solution:
First, using the laws of exponents, we can write

$$
-5{\text{i}}^{-1}=-\frac{5}{\text{i}}.
$$

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by $\text{i},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\text{i}}=-\frac{5}{\text{i}}\cdot \frac{\text{i}}{\text{i}}=-\frac{5\text{i}}{{\text{i}}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now recall that ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
-\frac{5\text{i}}{{\text{i}}^{2}}=-\frac{5\text{i}}{(-1)}=-\frac{5}{(-1)}\cdot \text{i}=5\text{i}.
$$

Question 9
?

8i−1=

a
−8
b
−8i
c
8i
d
18i
e
−18i
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, using the laws of exponents, we can write

8i−1=8i.

Multiplying the numerator and denominator by i, we get

8i=8i⋅ii=8ii2.

We now recall that i2=−1. Therefore,

8ii2=8i(−1)=8(−1)⋅i=−8i.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)-4 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3s-4}{s(s-2)},\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=$ {{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)-4\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-4L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-3=2{X}_{1}(s)-\frac{4}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-0={X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-3 & =2{X}_{1}(s)-\frac{4}{s} \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3-\frac{4}{s} \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3s-4}{s} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3s-4}{s(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s) & ={X}_{1}(s)+{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-1){X}_{2}(s) & ={X}_{1}(s) \\ (s-1){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3s-4}{s(s-2)} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3s-4}{s(s-1)(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system  in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3s-4}{s(s-2)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{3s-4}{s(s-1)(s-2)}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)-3 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2s-3}{s(s-4)}$ ,$\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{4{x}_{1}(t)-3\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=4L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-3L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+2L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-2=4{X}_{1}(s)-\frac{3}{s} \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+1=-{X}_{1}(s)+2{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-2 & =4{X}_{1}(s)-\frac{3}{s} \\ (s-4){X}_{1}(s) & =2-\frac{3}{s} \\ (s-4){X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2s-3}{s} \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{2s-3}{s(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)+1 & =-{X}_{1}(s)+2{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{2}(s) & =-{X}_{1}(s)-1 \\ (s-2){X}_{2}(s) & =-(\frac{2s-3}{s(s-4)})-1 \\ (s-2){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{-(2s-3)-s(s-4)}{s(s-4)} \\ (s-2){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{-2s+3-{s}^{2}+4s}{s(s-4)} \\ (s-2){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{-{s}^{2}+2s+3}{s(s-4)} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{-{s}^{2}+2s+3}{s(s-2)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2s-3}{s(s-4)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{-{s}^{2}+2s+3}{s(s-2)(s-4)}.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)+4 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)-5,\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution $$ {X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}=\frac{1}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}=-\frac{2}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{3}{s}. $$ Find the solution to the original initial value problem.
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}-\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}-2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={e}^{2\cdot t}-2\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{2t}-2 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{2}{s-2}+\frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{3}{s}\} \\  & =-2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-3}\}+3\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =-2{e}^{2\cdot t}+{e}^{3\cdot t}+3\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{3t}-2{e}^{2t}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}-2 \\ {e}^{3t}-2{e}^{2t}+3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To find ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to ${X}_{1}(s)$ and ${X}_{2}(s):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{2}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s-2}+\frac{2}{s}\} \\  & =-2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+1}\}+{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-2}\}+2\,{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & =-2{e}^{-1\cdot t}+{e}^{2\cdot t}+2 \\  & ={e}^{2t}+2-2{e}^{-t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s+1}\}-{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s}\} \\  & ={e}^{-1\cdot t}-1 \\  & =-1+{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What is the magnitude of the number $z=-13\text{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The imaginary number $-13\text{i}$ is equivalent to the complex number $z=0-13\text{i}.$

We know that for a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

So, the magnitude of $z=0-13\text{i}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|z| & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-13)^{2}} \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find $|z|$ if $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ where $x$ and $c$ are real numbers.
questions.worked_solution:
For a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

For the complex number $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ we have $a=2x$ and $b=4c.$ So, the magnitude is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}|2x+4c\text{i}| & =\sqrt{(2x)^{2}+(4c)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+16{c}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: What is the magnitude of the number $z=2\text{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The imaginary number $2\text{i}$ is equivalent to the complex number $z=0+2\text{i}.$

We know that for a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

So, the magnitude of $z=0+2\text{i}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|z| & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(2)^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

What is the magnitude of the number z=−13i?

a
−13
b
−13
c
13
d
−13
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The imaginary number −13i is equivalent to the complex number z=0−13i.

We know that for a complex number z=a+bi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=a2+b2.

So, the magnitude of z=0−13i is given by

|z|=a2+b2=(0)2+(−13)2=13.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Find $|z|$ if $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ where $x$ and $c$ are real numbers.
question.worked_solution:
For a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

For the complex number $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ we have $a=2x$ and $b=4c.$ So, the magnitude is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}|2x+4c\text{i}| & =\sqrt{(2x)^{2}+(4c)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+16{c}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Find |z| if z=2x+4ci, where x and c are real numbers.

a
4x2+16c2
b
2x2+4c2
c
2x2−4c2
d
2x2+4c2
e
4x2−16c2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a complex number z=a+bi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=a2+b2.

For the complex number z=2x+4ci, we have a=2x and b=4c. So, the magnitude is given by

|2x+4ci|=(2x)2+(4c)2=4x2+16c2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
For a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

For the complex number $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ we have $a=2x$ and $b=4c.$ So, the magnitude is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}|2x+4c\text{i}| & =\sqrt{(2x)^{2}+(4c)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+16{c}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Find |z| if z=2x+4ci, where x and c are real numbers.

a
4x2+16c2
b
2x2+4c2
c
2x2−4c2
d
2x2+4c2
e
4x2−16c2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a complex number z=a+bi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=a2+b2.

For the complex number z=2x+4ci, we have a=2x and b=4c. So, the magnitude is given by

|2x+4ci|=(2x)2+(4c)2=4x2+16c2.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Find $|z|$ if $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ where $x$ and $c$ are real numbers.
feedback.worked_solution:
For a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

For the complex number $z=2x+4c\text{i},$ we have $a=2x$ and $b=4c.$ So, the magnitude is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}|2x+4c\text{i}| & =\sqrt{(2x)^{2}+(4c)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+16{c}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: What is the magnitude of the number $z=2\text{i}?$
question.worked_solution:
The imaginary number $2\text{i}$ is equivalent to the complex number $z=0+2\text{i}.$

We know that for a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

So, the magnitude of $z=0+2\text{i}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|z| & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(2)^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The imaginary number 2i is equivalent to the complex number z=0+2i.

We know that for a complex number z=a+bi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=a2+b2.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
questions.raw_html:
1.Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=1. Given that the point P(1,1,0) lies on C, and that fx=3x+6xln⁡(xy), find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=3\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)-(x+y)^{3}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2x{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =2(\frac{1}{2}){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi /2)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =2(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=2x\end{aligned}
$$

4.Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=π. Given that the point P(12,π,1) lies on C, and that fx=2xecos⁡(xy)+sin⁡(xy), find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j+2\,k.$

5.Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=−2. Given that the point P(−2,2,3) lies on C, and that fy=x2y+2x−y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=1. Given that the point P(1,1,0) lies on C, and that fx=3x+6xln⁡(xy), find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

e

Submit
Correct

∂z∂x|(1,1)=3(1)+6(1)ln⁡(1⋅1)=3+6ln⁡1=3

z−z|(1,1)=∂z∂x|(1,1)(x−1)z−0=3(x−1)z=3x−3

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

a
j+2k
b
−2j+k
c
j+k
d
−j+2k
e
−j+k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=1. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(1,0).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (1,0):

fy(1,0)=3ln⁡(0+1)−(1+0)3=3⋅0−13=−1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,0)=fy(1,0)(y−0)z−(−1)=−1(y)z+1=−yz=−y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,0,−1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=1z=−y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=1, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=−y−1 (or y+z+1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,1,1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,1,1⟩=ijk100011=−j+k

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is −j+k.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j+2\,k.$

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=−2. Given that the point P(−2,2,3) lies on C, and that fy=x2y+2x−y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
j−3k
b
−2j+k
c
j+2k
d
3j+k
e
−2j+3k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=−2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(−2,2).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (−2,2):

fy(−2,2)=(−2)2(2)+2(−2)−(2)=8−4−2=2

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(−2,2)=fy(−2,2)(y−2)z−3=2(y−2)z=2y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(−2,2,3) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=−2z=2y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=−2, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=2y−1 (or 2y−z−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,2,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,2,−1⟩=ijk10002−1=j+2k

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is j+2k.

question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=1. Given that the point P(1,1,0) lies on C, and that fx=3x+6xln⁡(xy), find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
{y=1,z=4x−4
b
{y=1z=2x−2
c
{y=1z=3x
d
{y=1z=3x−3
e
{y=1z=2−2x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface z=f(x,y) with the plane y=1. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point P(1,1,0) will be given by the partial derivative ∂z∂x|(1,1).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ∂z∂x at (1,1):

∂z∂x|(1,1)=3(1)+6(1)ln⁡(1⋅1)=3+6ln⁡1=3

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−z|(1,1)=∂z∂x|(1,1)(x−1)z−0=3(x−1)z=3x−3

Finally, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,1,0) can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: {y=1z=3x−3

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

∂z∂x|(1,1)=3(1)+6(1)ln⁡(1⋅1)=3+6ln⁡1=3

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(y+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =(0+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2})+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1\cdot 0+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(\frac{1}{2},0)}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =1(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =x-\frac{1}{2} \\ z & =x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},0,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=3\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)-(x+y)^{3}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

b
−2j+k
c
j+k

−j+2k

−j+k

fy(1,0)=3ln⁡(0+1)−(1+0)3=3⋅0−13=−1

z−f(1,0)=fy(1,0)(y−0)z−(−1)=−1(y)z+1=−yz=−y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,0,−1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=1z=−y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=1, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=−y−1 (or y+z+1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,1,1⟩.

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,1,1⟩=ijk100011=−j+k

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2x{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =2(\frac{1}{2}){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi /2)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =2(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=2x\end{aligned}

last_observation.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =2(\frac{1}{2}){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi /2)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =2(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=2x\end{aligned}
$$

z−z|(1/2,π)=∂z∂x|(1/2,π)(x−12)z−1=2(x−12)z=2x

feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Given that the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=2x{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(\frac{1}{2},\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =2(\frac{1}{2}){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi /2)}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ={e}^{0}+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1/2,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1/2,\pi )}(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =2(x-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{1}{2},\pi ,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=2x\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-2,2).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,2) & ={f}_{y}(-2,2)(y-2) \\ z-3 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-1$ (or $2y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $j+2\,k.$

Question 5
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=−2. Given that the point P(−2,2,3) lies on C, and that fy=x2y+2x−y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
j−3k
b
−2j+k
c
j+2k
d
3j+k
e
−2j+3k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=−2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(−2,2).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (−2,2):

fy(−2,2)=(−2)2(2)+2(−2)−(2)=8−4−2=2

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(−2,2)=fy(−2,2)(y−2)z−3=2(y−2)z=2y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(−2,2,3) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=−2z=2y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=−2, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=2y−1 (or 2y−z−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,2,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,2,−1⟩=ijk10002−1=j+2k

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is j+2k.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14199122/assets/0a85b0be5f8e5db2cf4d1716e4afe4a2780c500d94a1ce282a9d0044f93ba084.png)

Consider the plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=\sqrt{3}$ and the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{6}{x}.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{6}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}(\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}) \\  & =(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =10-4\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le 1\}$
with mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=x{y}^{2}\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},$ where $x$ and $y$ area measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{4}x{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{6}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-0 \\  & =1.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $x$-axis is $1.2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3\}$
with mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=(x+y)\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},$ where $x$ and $y$ area measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+\frac{8y}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[4y+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =12+12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $y$-axis is $24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 3=3.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{7}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{7M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{7M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 2=6.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{13M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$

questions.raw_html:
5.Calculating the Moment of Inertia of a Lamina With Uniform Mass Density?

A rectangular plate of mass Mkg and uniform mass density occupies the region D={(x,y):1≤x≤4,1≤y≤3}, where x and y are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the x-axis.

E
Wed, Oct 14th @ 3:49 AM|Elapsed: 0:14Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{6}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}(\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}) \\  & =(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =10-4\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14199122/assets/0a85b0be5f8e5db2cf4d1716e4afe4a2780c500d94a1ce282a9d0044f93ba084.png)

Consider the plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=\sqrt{3}$ and the polar rays $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{6}{x}.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{6}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}(\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}) \\  & =(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =10-4\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
